transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. [Name]. Well, I guess... mostly I’m here because I’m just so incredibly tired. And I don't mean just needing a quick nap or something. It's like I'm tired in a way that sleep just doesn’t fix at all. I could sleep for hours and hours, and I still wake up feeling like my limbs are made of lead and my battery is completely dead. 

It’s actually getting kind of ridiculous because even the absolute smallest things feel totally overwhelming to me right now. Like, the other day, I was looking at the dishwasher, and all I had to do was unload it. It was just plates and some mugs, you know, a five-minute task tops, but I just stood there in the kitchen and it felt like this massive, impossible chore. It was just too much, so I just left it open and walked away. 

And it's really messing with my plans, too, because I'm not working right now, but I've been taking this online certificate class—I have some college from a while back, so I thought this would be a really good way to get back into things and build my resume—and I sit down at my laptop to read the modules, and I just can't. The energy completely drains out of me. Just reading a few pages for the class feels like way too much effort, and I end up just staring at the screen feeling completely exhausted and foggy. I just don't understand why I have absolutely zero energy for basic life stuff right now, so I figured I really needed to come in and see what's going on, because I can't keep letting a load of clean dishes defeat me for three days straight.
Over the past couple of weeks, have you also been feeling down, sad, or losing interest and pleasure in things you used to enjoy?

Yeah, definitely. I mean, both, really. The feeling down part is definitely there, but honestly, it's the losing interest part that is really bothering me the most right now. It’s like I just completely stopped caring about all the things that usually make me feel like, well, *me*. 

Like, usually I’m a very creative person. I love sketching. I have this really nice leather-bound sketchbook that I normally carry everywhere with me, just doing quick ink studies of people or buildings or whatever catches my eye. But it’s just been sitting on my nightstand for weeks, completely untouched. I look at it and just feel... nothing. No spark at all. And I used to absolutely love going to gallery openings downtown. There's this local collective I follow, and they had a big opening last Friday. Normally, I would have been the first one there, chatting with the artists, looking at the new pieces, just soaking all of that energy in. But I just couldn't even fathom getting dressed for it. The thought of it just made me feel empty.

And it’s not just the art stuff, either, it’s my whole daily routine. I usually really enjoy cooking—like, actually taking the time to chop fresh vegetables and try complicated new recipes, putting on some music while I do it—but lately, I just don't care. It's just entirely unappealing. And my physical outlets are totally gone, too. I used to do yoga almost every morning just to stretch and center myself, and I haven't unrolled my mat in I don't even know how long. I even have a friend who I usually play tennis with on the weekends. She texted me a couple of times this week to try and book a court, and I just made up some excuse about being busy because I didn't want to explain that I just don't have even a single ounce of desire to pick up a racket. Which is so weird for me, because I usually really look forward to our matches. It’s just... everything feels so flat. It’s really unsettling to look at your own life and your own hobbies and just not want any part of them whatsoever.
How long have you been experiencing this combination of low energy, low mood, and loss of interest—has it been going on for a couple of weeks, or longer, like months or years?

Well, it's definitely been longer than a couple of weeks, that's for sure. I'd say this whole... quieter stretch, where everything just feels so heavy and I have absolutely zero interest in anything, it's been going on for about three months now. 

I remember specifically because it started right around the time my sister had her baby shower, which was early October. I was supposed to help her set up, you know, do all the balloon arches and arrange the little finger foods and everything, because I'm usually the one who loves doing all that creative hosting stuff. But I remember waking up that morning and just feeling this absolute wall of exhaustion hit me. I dragged myself there, but I was basically useless. I just sat in the corner the whole time feeling completely drained and like I couldn't even fake a smile for the photos. 

And since then, it’s just been this constant, steady decline into this flat, tired state. October just sort of blurred into November, and then the holidays came and went, and I barely even noticed them. Usually, I'm the first one to put up decorations and bake cookies—I have this amazing recipe for ginger molasses cookies that my grandmother gave me, and I usually make dozens of them to give out to my neighbors and friends. But this year? Nothing. I didn't even buy a single string of lights. 

So yeah, it's been a solid three months of just feeling like I'm moving through molasses. Every single day is just a repeat of waking up exhausted, staring at my sketchbook or my laptop, and just... doing nothing. It feels like an eternity, honestly, when you're just sitting in it day after day, watching the weeks tick by while you can't even muster the energy to unload the dishwasher.
Besides the fatigue and low mood, have you noticed any physical changes recently—like feeling unusually cold, gaining weight without changes in eating, or your skin or hair becoming dry or brittle?

Well, no, I wouldn't say I've felt unusually cold or anything like that. And my hair and skin seem pretty normal, I guess. But you mentioned weight, and actually, it's funny you bring that up because it's kind of been the exact opposite of gaining weight. 

I was getting dressed the other day—well, trying to, anyway, since getting dressed feels like a monumental task lately—and I put on this pair of jeans that I wear all the time. They're my favorite pair, you know, the ones that usually fit just perfectly, and they were just hanging off me. I had to go digging through the back of my closet to find a belt, which I haven't worn with those jeans in years. 

And it's not like I'm trying to lose weight or on some new diet or doing any of those intense workout programs. Like I said, I haven't even unrolled my yoga mat in months. It's just... my appetite has been completely off. It’s like the thought of food is just as exhausting as everything else. I'll go through almost the whole day, and then around four or five in the afternoon, I'll suddenly realize that literally all I've had to consume since I woke up was a cup of coffee and maybe, I don't know, a couple of bites of a piece of toast or a handful of crackers. 

I just don't have the desire to eat. Usually, I'm the kind of person who plans out meals, goes to the farmer's market on Sunday mornings to get fresh produce, and really enjoys the whole process of cooking and eating. I have this whole collection of spices that I usually love experimenting with. But right now, even the idea of deciding what to eat, let alone actually preparing it and chewing it, just feels like too much work. So I just skip it. I guess it makes sense that my clothes are getting looser when I'm basically running on caffeine and a few random bites of whatever is easiest to grab without actually having to prepare anything.
Have you ever had a period like this before—weeks or months of low mood, low energy, and loss of interest—at any point earlier in your life?

No... no, I really haven't. And I think that's why it's freaking me out so much, to be perfectly honest. 

I mean, sure, I've had bad days or even a bad week here and there. Everyone gets sad, right? Like, back in my twenties when I was taking classes at the community college and trying to figure out what I wanted to do with my life, I'd get stressed out. Or when I went through a really bad breakup a few years ago—I was definitely sad then. I cried, I stayed in bed for a weekend, watched a bunch of sad movies, ate way too much takeout... the whole cliché, you know? But that felt normal. It made sense because there was a reason for it, and it passed. I always bounced back. I still wanted to talk to my friends, I still wanted to go outside eventually.

I've always been a really active, engaged person. Even without a traditional 9-to-5 job right now, I'm usually always doing *something*—volunteering, painting, helping friends, just constantly on the move and involved in things. So this? This absolute flatline where I can't even get off the couch for months? It's completely uncharted territory for me. 

I keep looking back, trying to think if maybe I felt like this in high school or something, but I just didn't. I've never had this... this total absence of caring about anything. It's like I'm a completely different person than I have been for my entire thirty-three years of existence. I've always been the one with the ideas and the plans, the one dragging other people out of the house. So to just be sitting here, day after day, week after week, with absolutely nothing in the tank... it's never happened before. Not once. I just keep waiting to wake up and feel like myself again, but it's just not happening.
During these past three months, have you had any thoughts of hurting yourself or wishing you weren't alive?

No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I know that's a thing people go through when they get really depressed, and I've seen documentaries about it and read articles where people talk about how they just wanted to escape it all. But for me, it's not like that at all. 

It's more just... I'm so incredibly tired of being tired, if that makes sense? Like, I just want this specific feeling to stop. I don't want to not be here. I actually really want to be here, I want to be doing all the things I usually do! I keep looking at my painting supplies sitting in the corner of the living room—I have this whole setup, this beautiful wooden easel I got at an estate sale a few years ago, and all these acrylics and oils that I usually love mixing and playing with. I look at them and I think, "I should go paint." But then the thought of getting up, walking over there, opening the tubes, cleaning the brushes afterward... it's just too much. 

But I've never once thought about hurting myself or, you know, ending things. It's not a desire to disappear, it's just a complete lack of energy to participate in the life I already have. Sometimes I'll just lie there on the couch, staring at the ceiling fan—which, by the way, has a wobble that I usually would have fixed by now because I'm pretty handy like that, I usually fix all the little things around the apartment—and I just think about how frustrating it is that I can't just snap out of it. 

I just want to get back to normal. I want to wake up and feel like making coffee and actually drinking it while it's hot, instead of letting it sit on the counter until it's room temperature and then just pouring it down the drain. I want to want to do things again. So, no, definitely no thoughts of hurting myself. Just... a lot of frustration that I'm stuck in this weird, heavy holding pattern and I can't seem to find the exit.

Over these past few months, has this affected your ability to manage basic day-to-day self-care—like showering, getting dressed, or leaving your apartment—or have you still been able to keep up with those things most days?

Well, like I was saying earlier about getting dressed, it really has become this huge, monumental task. And showering is pretty much the same story. I mean, I’ll literally just sit on the edge of the bathtub for twenty minutes, staring at the grout, trying to convince myself to just turn the water on, and half the time I just give up and put my pajamas right back on. Leaving the apartment? Forget it. I barely even go down to check the mail anymore. 

And it’s just bleeding into absolutely everything else in my life. I’m actually supposed to be doing this certificate coursework right now—which I was really excited about when I signed up—but I’ve fallen completely behind. I usually have this whole system, you know? A color-coded planner, a dedicated study time, the whole nine yards. But lately, I just can’t keep my plans organized or follow through on anything consistently. I’ll open the laptop, look at the modules I'm supposed to read, and just close it again because my brain just won't cooperate. 

It’s the exact same with everything around the house. The bills are just piling up on the kitchen counter. The household tasks are completely neglected. Like, the laundry is a literal mountain in the corner of the bedroom. My spouse has honestly been an absolute saint through all of this, because they’ve had to step in and do so much more at home. They're handling the meals, the chores, making sure things don't fall apart. I feel incredibly guilty about it, because we usually have a really good, equal partnership, but I’m just useless right now. 

And because I can't even get myself out the door, I’ve completely pulled back from my friends. We usually have this standing Thursday get-together, and I’ve canceled so many times in a row that I don't even know what to say to them anymore. I’ve even dropped out of the art commitments I normally care so much about. I was supposed to contribute to this local project, and I just had to back out. I just couldn't do it. So, yeah, I guess you could say my ability to keep up with my normal day-to-day life is pretty much non-existent right now. Everything is just piling up while I sit on the couch.

Like, back in my twenties when I was taking classes at the community college and trying to figure out what I wanted to do with my life, I'd get stressed out. Or when I went through a really bad breakup a few years ago—I was definitely sad then. I cried, I stayed in bed for a weekend, watched a bunch of sad movies, ate way too much takeout... the whole cliché, you know? But that felt normal. It made sense because there was a reason for it, and it passed. I always bounced back. I still wanted to talk to my friends, I still wanted to go outside eventually.

I've always been a really active, engaged person. Even without a traditional 9-to-5 job right now, I'm usually always doing *something*—volunteering, painting, helping friends, just constantly on the move and involved in things. So this? This absolute flatline where I can't even get off the couch for months? It's completely uncharted territory for me. 

I keep looking back, trying to think if maybe I felt like this in high school or something, but I just didn't. I've never had this... this total absence of caring about anything. It's like I'm a completely different person than I have been for my entire thirty-three years of existence. I've always been the one with the ideas and the plans, the one dragging other people out of the house. So to just be sitting here, day after day, week after week, with absolutely nothing in the tank... it's never happened before. Not once. I just keep waiting to wake up and feel like myself again, but it's just not happening.

inference.note: First depressive episode confirmed (no prior episodes of mania, hypomania, or depression), ruling out recurrent depressive disorder (F33.9). Hypothyroidism also less likely given no cold intolerance, weight loss instead of gain, normal skin/hair.

doctor.intent: Assess for suicidal ideation or thoughts of self-harm, which is critical for safety assessment and determining severity of the depressive episode.
doctor.question: During these past three months, have you had any thoughts of hurting yourself or wishing you weren't alive?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about suicidal thoughts or ideation, which is not included in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I know that's a thing people go through when they get really depressed, and I've seen documentaries about it and read articles where people talk about how they just wanted to escape it all. But for me, it's not like that at all. 

It's more just... I'm so incredibly tired of being tired, if that makes sense? Like, I just want this specific feeling to stop. I don't want to not be here. I actually really want to be here, I want to be doing all the things I usually do! I keep looking at my painting supplies sitting in the corner of the living room—I have this whole setup, this beautiful wooden easel I got at an estate sale a few years ago, and all these acrylics and oils that I usually love mixing and playing with. I look at them and I think, "I should go paint." But then the thought of getting up, walking over there, opening the tubes, cleaning the brushes afterward... it's just too much. 

But I've never once thought about hurting myself or, you know, ending things. It's not a desire to disappear, it's just a complete lack of energy to participate in the life I already have. Sometimes I'll just lie there on the couch, staring at the ceiling fan—which, by the way, has a wobble that I usually would have fixed by now because I'm pretty handy like that, I usually fix all the little things around the apartment—and I just think about how frustrating it is that I can't just snap out of it. 

I just want to get back to normal. I want to wake up and feel like making coffee and actually drinking it while it's hot, instead of letting it sit on the counter until it's room temperature and then just pouring it down the drain. I want to want to do things again. So, no, definitely no thoughts of hurting myself. Just... a lot of frustration that I'm stuck in this weird, heavy holding pattern and I can't seem to find the exit.

inference.note: Confirmed first-ever depressive episode (~3 months) with pervasive anhedonia, fatigue, hypersomnia, appetite/weight loss, and no prior mood episodes or suicidal ideation—consistent with a major depressive episode. Retained F32.9 but added F32.1/F32.2 to reflect possible moderate-to-severe symptom burden pending further clarification of functional impairment and psychotic features.

doctor.intent: Assess the degree of functional impairment (e.g., ability to manage basic self-care, leave the house, or interact with others) to determine whether the episode is of moderate or severe severity
doctor.question: Over these past few months, has this affected your ability to manage basic day-to-day self-care—like showering, getting dressed, or leaving your apartment—or have you still been able to keep up with those things most days?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’ve fallen behind in my certificate coursework and let bills, meals, and household tasks pile up because I can’t keep my plans organized or follow through consistently. My spouse has had to step in more at home, and I’ve pulled back from friends and art commitments I normally care about.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how the symptoms have affected my ability to manage day-to-day tasks and self-care, which corresponds to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Well, like I was saying earlier about getting dressed, it really has become this huge, monumental task. And showering is pretty much the same story. I mean, I’ll literally just sit on the edge of the bathtub for twenty minutes, staring at the grout, trying to convince myself to just turn the water on, and half the time I just give up and put my pajamas right back on. Leaving the apartment? Forget it. I barely even go down to check the mail anymore. 

And it’s just bleeding into absolutely everything else in my life. I’m actually supposed to be doing this certificate coursework right now—which I was really excited about when I signed up—but I’ve fallen completely behind. I usually have this whole system, you know? A color-coded planner, a dedicated study time, the whole nine yards. But lately, I just can’t keep my plans organized or follow through on anything consistently. I’ll open the laptop, look at the modules I'm supposed to read, and just close it again because my brain just won't cooperate. 

It’s the exact same with everything around the house. The bills are just piling up on the kitchen counter. The household tasks are completely neglected. Like, the laundry is a literal mountain in the corner of the bedroom. My spouse has honestly been an absolute saint through all of this, because they’ve had to step in and do so much more at home. They're handling the meals, the chores, making sure things don't fall apart. I feel incredibly guilty about it, because we usually have a really good, equal partnership, but I’m just useless right now. 

And because I can't even get myself out the door, I’ve completely pulled back from my friends. We usually have this standing Thursday get-together, and I’ve canceled so many times in a row that I don't even know what to say to them anymore. I’ve even dropped out of the art commitments I normally care so much about. I was supposed to contribute to this local project, and I just had to back out. I just couldn't do it. So, yeah, I guess you could say my ability to keep up with my normal day-to-day life is pretty much non-existent right now. Everything is just piling up while I sit on the couch.

inference.note: No prior depressive episodes, no manic/hypomanic history, no suicidal ideation, but severe functional impairment (unable to shower, dress, manage self-care, complete coursework, withdrawal from all activities) with significant anhedonia, fatigue, appetite/weight loss lasting 3 months. Severity of impairment without psychotic features points to a single severe depressive episode without psychotic features (F32.2), ruling out F32.1 (moderate) and F32.9 (unspecified) given the clear severity and duration now established.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with a single, first-ever episode (no prior history) of depressed mood, profound anhedonia, and severe fatigue lasting ~3 months, meeting core MDE criteria. Associated symptoms include significant unintentional weight loss/appetite loss, psychomotor slowing, and marked impairment in self-care, occupational (coursework), household, and social functioning severe enough to require spousal caretaking. No psychotic features (no hallucinations/delusions) and explicitly denies suicidal ideation, distinguishing severe-without-psychotic-features (F32.2) from psychotic (F32.3) or moderate (F32.1) presentations. Hypothyroidism (E03.9) was considered given fatigue/appetite change but ruled out as the patient denies cold intolerance, weight gain, or skin/hair changes, and there is no prior mood episode history suggesting bipolar course.
